passage: The last bus had left, and the small-town school was quiet except for a crow on the roof. Rekha still could not see how three-fourths and six-eighths could be the same. Charu Madam, the fractions teacher, had stayed on after the bell, drawing circles on the slate with a stub of chalk. "Cut this one in four, that one in eight. See?" Rekha counted the pieces, then grinned. "They are equal!" Madam smiled and said, "Take your time." When Rekha's uncle came to walk her home, she said, "Thank you, Madam," and next day was first to finish the homework.

qa.q: What did Charu Madam draw the circles on?
qa.a: She drew circles on the slate with a stub of chalk.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she counted the pieces and grinned?
qa.a: She felt relieved and proud that she finally understood, and she also felt cared for by her teacher who stayed on.

qa.q: What did Rekha do to show her gratitude?
qa.a: She said thank you and worked harder, becoming the first to finish the homework the next day.

qa.q: How might Charu Madam have felt seeing Rekha's grin?
qa.a: She probably felt satisfied and glad that staying late had helped, though she was also tired after school.

grounding: A teacher stays late to help a child understand fractions; the child feels cared for, says thank you and tries harder.

passage: 'Aditi, you said Ma'am stayed back to explain fractions? That reminds your Irfan Chacha of something. In Class 5, I was sure I was hopeless at fractions. Everyone else seemed to understand pizza slices, and I just saw circles. One evening Sharma Sir kept me after school. The other teachers had gone home; the peon was locking doors. He cut a guava into halves, quarters and eighths on his desk and let me eat each piece I got right. By sunset I'd eaten most of the guava and understood it all. I said thank you so many times he laughed. After that I worked twice as hard, not because I was scared of him, but because he believed I could.'

qa.q: What did Sharma Sir cut on his desk?
qa.a: A guava, into halves, quarters and eighths.

qa.q: How did young Irfan feel about fractions before that evening?
qa.a: Discouraged and hopeless, because everyone else seemed to understand and he just saw circles.

qa.q: What choice did young Irfan make after the evening with Sharma Sir, and why?
qa.a: He thanked him warmly and worked twice as hard, because feeling believed in gave him confidence.

qa.q: How might Sharma Sir have felt when Irfan kept saying thank you?
qa.a: Amused and pleased; he laughed, glad his extra time had helped 😊

grounding: An uncle recalls a teacher who stayed late to teach him fractions, and how feeling cared for made him try harder.

passage: The storm knocked out the power just as the last bell rang, and Vijay's father phoned to say he'd be an hour late because the roads were flooded. Aparna Ma'am could have gone to the staffroom. Instead she pulled a bench to the window, where there was still grey light. 'Show me your fraction homework, the one you left blank.' Vijay's ears went hot. 'I don't get it.' 'Then let's get it.' She drew rotis on the back of an old notice, and they folded paper strips into halves and thirds. Thunder rolled. By the time his father's scooter splashed up, Vijay had done five sums alone. 'Thank you, Ma'am,' he said, and meant it with his whole chest. At home he did five more without being told.

qa.q: What did Aparna Ma'am draw on the back of an old notice?
How did Vijay feel when he thanked Aparna Ma'am?
qa.a: Deeply grateful and cared for; he meant it with his whole chest.

qa.q: What did Vijay do after that evening, and what does it show?
qa.a: He did five more sums at home without being told, showing new confidence from feeling supported.

qa.q: Why might Aparna Ma'am have used the wait for fractions?
qa.a: She saw he had left the homework blank and cared enough to help instead of resting in the staffroom.

grounding: During a stormy wait a teacher stays to help a boy with fractions, and he feels cared for, thanks her and tries harder.
